summary:
Our dashboard is an interactive 3D web app that helps researches and the public see which microgravity fire-safety investigations matters for a given crewed environment. NASA has run many fire experiments in orbit, but the results are not very accessible and hard to visualize to understand the fire safety implications. We gathered ten investigation groups from NASA's Combustion Science investigations and summarized each one. This includes what was done, what the data shows, and what the data leads towards in terms of research. We then self scored each group's relevance to fire safety (0–3 with a reason) for six habitable environments: the Space Station, a spacecraft, a lunar habitat, a Mars habitat, a pressurized rover, and a spacesuit. Additionally, relevant publications based on each study are also highlighted in the app. 

Users can free explore 3D scenarios, investigation summaries, data, and relevant research, ask questions to an embedded SI chatbot, or experience a guided walkthrough with a subtitles using the story button at the top right. 

We believe this combination of SI powered features, interactive 3D scenarios, and accessible data visuals, makes our project uniquely accessible and fun to use for anyone from the average curious learner to a mission planner. On top of that, it is still extremely effective when it comes to presenting NASA's combustion science research in a comprehensive manner.
details:
What it does:

A welcome screen asks "Where will your crew live?" and offers six environments. A short coach-mark tour then introduces the panels.

Each environment has a 3D scene with clickable hotspots:

  • Cygnus with the Saffire unit and a burning sample
  • The distant ISS
  • Low-poly concept scenes for the spacecraft, lunar base, Mars base, rover and spacesuit

An experiment list shows all ten investigation groups, each scored 0–3 for the current environment with a short reason. They are tagged by fire-safety pillars: prevention, detection or suppression.

A detail drawer covers each investigation:

  • Objectives, process, key findings and advances, each with paper citations
  • Fuels, sample geometry, hardware and instruments
  • Test conditions compared with the current environment's air
  • What changed between tests and what stayed the same
  • Related investigations and follow-up research papers

A compare view puts two investigations side by side and highlights the fuels and instruments they share.

Concept environments have topic cards. Each card states a problem in that environment and links it to the investigations it builds on and the best-ranked follow-up papers. Partial-gravity data gaps get their own badge.

An AI assistant chat panel streams answers grounded in the project data. Investigation IDs it cites become buttons that open that investigation.

How it works:

Frontend: Vite with React 19 and TypeScript. The 3D scenes use three.js through React Three Fiber, drei and postprocessing. UI motion uses Framer Motion, styling uses Tailwind CSS 4, and app state uses Zustand. All 3D geometry is built in code; no external models or textures are loaded.

Data pipeline: the team built spreadsheets in data:

  • Publication titles, abstracts and keywords for each PSI investigation (about 280 rows)
  • A ranking of 45 follow-up papers by overall fire-safety advancement
  • A ranking of the same papers within each need: flammability, detection, suppression, modeling, monitoring, cleanup and mask
  • TypeScript scripts turn these into the JSON the app reads.

Assistant backend: a small Node server keeps the model API key out of the browser. At startup it builds a cached system prompt from the project data and streams replies as newline-delimited JSON. It can use the Anthropic API (Claude) or Texas A&M's TAMU SI Chat gateway, and it applies rate limits and a cap on conversation length.

Benefits:

It turns scattered combustion literature into findings organized by environment, with sources attached.

It shows where data is missing, not only what is known. Partial-gravity fire data is one example.

It works for both experts and newcomers: plain-language summaries sit on top, and full citations are one click away.

We want a starting point that habitat and vehicle designers, students and the public can use to see how flames behave without gravity. It should show which past experiments apply to their mission and which questions still need new tests on the Moon or Mars.

Tools:

TypeScript, React, three.js and React Three Fiber, Vite, Tailwind, Zustand, Framer Motion, Node.js 22, the Anthropic SDK, ESLint, Prettier, Claude Code, Git and GitHub.

Note: All 3D assests used for our 3D viewer are unique assets created with SI, but since they are not technically images or videos they were not watermarked.
dataRefs: A researcher's guide to combustion science
